introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Further Mathematics Paper 2 (0775), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Duration: three hours.**

Answer ALL 10 questions. For your guidance, the approximate mark allocation for parts of each question is indicated. Mathematical formulae and tables published by the Board, and noiseless non-programmable electronic calculators are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage.
incertitudes: Question 6 : les deux demandes (« Show that... represents a hyperbola », 3 marks, et « Find in polar form the equations of the asymptotes », 5 marks) ne sont pas étiquetées dans le sujet ; elles sont codées a et b. « Polar form » est lu comme des droites θ = constante passant par le pôle, le centre de l'hyperbole étant l'origine.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Show that the curve with polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$ where,

$$r^2 = \frac{2}{1 - 3\sin^2\theta},$$

represents a hyperbola. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Multiply out the denominator:

$$r^2\left(1 - 3\sin^2\theta\right) = 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r^2 - 3\,(r\sin\theta)^2 = 2.$$

Convert to Cartesian coordinates with $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, $r^2 = x^2 + y^2$:

$$x^2 + y^2 - 3y^2 = 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^2 - 2y^2 = 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{y^2}{1} = 1.$$

This is of the standard form $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ with $a^2 = 2$ and $b^2 = 1$, so the curve is a hyperbola centred at the origin with transverse axis along the $x$-axis and vertices $(\pm\sqrt2, 0)$. $\blacksquare$

questions.enonce_markdown: Find in polar form, the equations of the asymptotes to this hyperbola. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Cartesian asymptotes.** For $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ the asymptotes are $y = \pm\dfrac{b}{a}x$. Here $a = \sqrt2$, $b = 1$:

$$y = \pm\frac{x}{\sqrt2}.$$

(Equivalently, set the right-hand side of $x^2 - 2y^2 = 2$ to $0$: $x^2 - 2y^2 = 0$, so $y = \pm\dfrac{x}{\sqrt2}$.)

**Polar form.** These lines pass through the pole (the centre of the hyperbola), so in polar form they are the lines $\theta = \text{constant}$ with $\tan\theta = \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$:

$$\boxed{\theta = \alpha \quad\text{and}\quad \theta = -\alpha, \qquad \alpha = \arctan\frac{1}{\sqrt2} \approx 0.615\ \text{rad}\ (35.3^\circ)}$$

(Each line is also described by adding $\pi$ to the angle; for example the second line is also $\theta = \pi - \alpha$.)

**Confirmation from the polar equation.** $r \to \infty$ exactly when the denominator $1 - 3\sin^2\theta \to 0^+$, that is $\sin^2\theta = \tfrac13$, $\sin\theta = \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$. Then $\cos^2\theta = \tfrac23$, so $\tan^2\theta = \dfrac{1/3}{2/3} = \tfrac12$, which gives the same directions $\tan\theta = \pm\dfrac1{\sqrt2}$. Also $r^2 > 0$ requires $3\sin^2\theta < 1$: the curve exists only for $\theta$ close to $0$ or to $\pi$ (the two branches), bounded by these asymptotic directions.
